facts: The castle stands on the site of an original Roman fort, with sections of Roman wall still visible.
Its Victorian Gothic interiors were designed by architect William Burges for the 3rd Marquess of Bute.
The castle keep dates from the 12th century, built on a Norman motte.
It was the first major stadium in the UK with a fully retractable roof, completed in 1999.
It is the home of the Wales national rugby union team.
The stadium sits right beside the River Taff in the centre of Cardiff.
Caerphilly Castle is the largest castle in Wales and the second-largest in Britain after Windsor.
It was built by Gilbert de Clare in the late 13th century and pioneered concentric castle design in Britain.
One of its towers leans further than the Leaning Tower of Pisa, a result of subsidence and Civil War damage.
Chepstow Castle is considered the oldest surviving post-Roman stone fortification in Britain, begun in 1067.
It overlooks the River Wye close to where it meets the Severn Estuary.
The castle was built to secure a key crossing point into Wales soon after the Norman Conquest.
Tenby retains substantial sections of its 13th-century town walls.
The town's colourful Georgian harbourfront houses are among the most photographed in Wales.
Boats from Tenby harbour run to Caldey Island, home to a working monastery.
Pembroke Castle was the birthplace of Henry Tudor, later King Henry VII, in 1457.
Its Great Keep, over 24 metres tall, is one of the finest surviving examples in Britain.
The castle sits on a rocky promontory above the Pembroke River.
Milford Haven is one of the deepest natural harbours in the world.
It has been a major oil and gas terminal for the UK since the 1960s.
The town itself was purpose-built in the 1790s to a grid-street plan by Quaker whalers from Nantucket.
St Davids, reached from Haverfordwest, is Britain's smallest city, named for Wales' patron saint.
The cathedral was founded in the 12th century on the site of a 6th-century monastery.
Haverfordwest is the nearest railhead, with St Davids reached onward by road.
The park is built around the former Lewis Merthyr Colliery, which closed in 1983.
It tells the story of coal mining in the Rhondda Valleys, once one of the world's most productive coalfields.
Trehafod station serves the heritage park directly.
Big Pit, at Blaenavon, allows visitors to descend 90 metres underground with former miners as guides.
Blaenavon's industrial landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage Site for its role in the Industrial Revolution.
Ebbw Vale Town is the nearest railhead, on a line reopened to passengers in 2008.
Cyfarthfa Castle was built in 1825 by ironmaster William Crawshay II, overlooking his ironworks.
Merthyr Tydfil was the world's leading iron-producing town in the early 19th century.
The town gave its name to the Merthyr Rising of 1831, an early workers' uprising.
Margam Park is built around the ruins of a 12th-century Cistercian abbey and a Victorian Gothic mansion.
The park is home to a large herd of fallow deer.
Port Talbot Parkway sits close to one of the largest steelworks in the UK.
The Gower was the first area in Britain to be designated an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, in 1956.
Its coastline includes Rhossili Bay, regularly ranked among the best beaches in the world.
Gowerton station sits on the edge of the peninsula, on the Swansea to Carmarthen line.
The museum tells the story of industry and innovation in Wales, in the city's former maritime quarter.
Swansea was known as 'Copperopolis' in the 19th century for its dominance of the global copper trade.
Poet Dylan Thomas was born and grew up in Swansea.
Kidwelly Castle is one of the best-preserved examples of a Norman 'walls within walls' concentric castle.
It overlooks the River Gwendraeth and was refortified several times over 400 years.
The castle featured as a filming location for the 2004 film King Arthur.
Carmarthen is widely regarded as the oldest continuously occupied town in Wales.
Its Roman amphitheatre, Moridunum, could once hold around 4,500 spectators.
Carmarthen is the western terminus of the main line from London Paddington via the Wales Coast route.
Dinefwr was the seat of the medieval princes of Deheubarth, an independent Welsh kingdom.
The surrounding parkland is home to an ancient herd of white park cattle.
Llandeilo station sits on the scenic Heart of Wales line.

landmark: Heart of Wales Line scenery (Sugar Loaf)
facts: Sugar Loaf is one of the most remote request stops in Britain, with only a handful of trains a day.
The Heart of Wales line runs 121 miles between Shrewsbury and Swansea through sparsely populated countryside.
Sugar Loaf station has no road access and is reached only on foot.

landmark: Llandrindod Wells spa heritage (via Builth Road)
facts: Llandrindod Wells grew into a fashionable Victorian spa town after its mineral springs were promoted from the 1860s.
Builth Road is the nearest station on the Heart of Wales line, some distance from Llandrindod itself.
The wider area hosts the Royal Welsh Show, Wales' largest agricultural event, each July.
Llanwrtyd Wells is often cited as the smallest town in Britain by population.
It hosts eccentric annual events including the World Bog Snorkelling Championships.
The town developed as a spa resort after a sulphur well was discovered in the 18th century.
Cynghordy Viaduct is one of the largest structures on the Heart of Wales line, with 18 arches.
It stands around 31 metres above the valley floor.
The viaduct was completed in 1868 as part of the line linking Llandovery and Llanwrtyd.
Llandovery's ruined castle overlooks the River Tywi from a mound above the town.
A striking modern steel sculpture of Welsh prince Llywelyn ap Gruffudd Fychan stands by the castle.
The town has long been a sheep and cattle market centre for rural Carmarthenshire.
Neath Abbey was once described by the antiquarian John Leland as the fairest abbey in all Wales.
It was founded in 1130 for Savigniac, later Cistercian, monks.
Neath sits at the mouth of the Vale of Neath, on the edge of the South Wales coalfield.
Barry Island became a major seaside resort after the Barry Railway reached it in the 1890s.
Whitmore Bay, its main beach, has featured prominently as a filming location for the TV series Gavin & Stacey.
Barry Island is technically a peninsula rather than a true island.
The Severn Tunnel, completed in 1886, was the longest mainline railway tunnel in Britain for over a century.
It runs beneath the Severn Estuary, connecting Severn Tunnel Junction towards Bristol.
The estuary itself has one of the highest tidal ranges in the world.
Fishguard Harbour station connects directly to ferry services to Rosslare in Ireland.
The port was the site of the last invasion of mainland Britain, a failed French landing in 1797.
Fishguard's harbour was built in the early 20th century partly to support transatlantic liner traffic.
The Transporter Bridge, opened in 1906, carries a moving gondola across the River Usk rather than a conventional deck.
It is one of only a handful of working transporter bridges left in the world.
Newport was historically one of the busiest coal-exporting ports in South Wales.
Pontypridd is regarded as the birthplace of the Welsh rugby anthem 'Bread of Heaven', linked to the town's chapels.
The Old Bridge over the River Taff, built in 1756, was the longest single-span stone bridge in the world at the time.
Ynysangharad Park includes a lido and war memorial overlooking the town.
Abergavenny is often called the gateway to the Brecon Beacons (Bannau Brycheiniog) National Park.
The town's ruined castle was the site of a notorious 1175 massacre of Welsh lords.
Abergavenny hosts one of the UK's leading food festivals each September.
Penarth Pier opened in 1895 and remains one of the best-preserved Victorian piers in Wales.
The town developed as a genteel seaside resort for wealthy Cardiff residents in the 19th century.
Penarth overlooks the Severn Estuary towards Weston-super-Mare.
Llantwit Major is home to one of the oldest religious and educational centres in Britain, founded around 500 AD.
Nearby Dunraven Bay is known for its dramatic limestone cliffs on the Glamorgan Heritage Coast.
The town's parish church holds an important collection of early Celtic Christian stones.
Llanelli is nicknamed 'Tinopolis' for its historic dominance of the tinplate industry.
The Scarlets rugby team, based at Parc y Scarlets, is one of Wales' most storied clubs.
Llanelli famously beat the All Blacks in a legendary 1972 match.
Saundersfoot's harbour was originally built to export coal and iron ore in the 19th century.
The village's sheltered beach makes it a popular Pembrokeshire holiday resort today.
The Pembrokeshire Coast Path passes directly through the village.
Bridgend takes its name from an ancient bridge crossing the River Ogmore.
The town sits at the junction of the South Wales Main Line and the line to Maesteg.
Nearby Ogmore Castle and Coity Castle reflect the area's Norman conquest history.
Cwmbran was designated one of Britain's first post-war new towns in 1949.
It grew from a collection of industrial villages into a planned urban centre.
Cwmbran railway station reopened in 1986 after earlier station closures in the area.
Llansamlet lies at the southern end of the Swansea Valley, once heavily industrialised with copper and coal works.
The area has been substantially redeveloped as a retail and business park since the late 20th century.
Llansamlet station serves the northeastern suburbs of Swansea.
Whitland was historically the site of a great assembly of Welsh law under Hywel Dda in the 10th century.
The town remains a junction station where the Pembroke Dock branch leaves the main line.
Whitland was once a hub for the local dairy and creamery industry.
Narberth's ruined castle is linked to tales in the medieval Welsh mythological collection, the Mabinogion.
The town has become known for its independent shops and food scene.
Narberth sits close to the boundary of the Pembrokeshire Coast National Park.
Cardiff Bay was transformed from a former coal-exporting dock into a waterfront district in the 1990s and 2000s.
The Senedd, home to the Welsh Parliament, opened on the waterfront in 2006.
Cardiff Bay station is the terminus of a short branch line from Cardiff Queen Street.
Llangadog sits in the fertile Tywi Valley, one of the longest rivers entirely within Wales.
The village is a small stop on the scenic Heart of Wales line between Llandeilo and Llandovery.
The surrounding area is known for dairy farming and the nearby Brecon Beacons foothills.
Conwy Castle was built by Edward I between 1283 and 1287 as part of his conquest of Wales.
It forms a UNESCO World Heritage Site alongside Conwy's near-complete medieval town walls.
Conwy station sits directly beside the castle and the town walls.
The Great Orme is a large limestone headland overlooking Llandudno, reached by cable car or tramway.
Llandudno developed as a planned Victorian seaside resort from the 1850s onwards.
The town inspired part of Lewis Carroll's Alice in Wonderland, after his friendship with a local family.
Bangor Pier, opened in 1896, is one of the longest piers in Wales at over 460 metres.
Bangor is Wales' oldest city, with a cathedral tradition dating back to the 6th century.
The city sits on the Menai Strait, opposite the island of Anglesey.
South Stack Lighthouse stands on a small island off Holy Island, reached by a bridge and steep steps.
Holyhead is the main ferry port linking Wales to Dublin, Ireland.
Holyhead sits on Holy Island, connected to the rest of Anglesey by a causeway.
Blaenau Ffestiniog was once the centre of the largest slate-mining industry in the world.
The surrounding slate landscape of northwest Wales is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The town connects to the heritage Ffestiniog Railway, which once carried slate down to Porthmadog.
Betws-y-Coed is a popular gateway village for Eryri (Snowdonia) National Park.
Nearby Swallow Falls is one of the highest-volume waterfalls in Wales.
The village became a favoured retreat for Victorian landscape painters.
Harlech Castle, another Edward I fortress, forms part of the same UNESCO World Heritage listing as Conwy.
A famous Welsh song commemorates a legendary long siege of the castle.
The castle originally stood right by the sea, though the coastline has since receded.

landmark: Aberystwyth seafront & the National Library of Wales
facts: The National Library of Wales, overlooking the town, holds the country's most important collection of Welsh books and manuscripts.
Aberystwyth is the terminus of the Cambrian Line from Shrewsbury.
The town's Victorian pier and cliff railway are among Wales' oldest seaside attractions.
The Centre for Alternative Technology, near Machynlleth, has demonstrated eco-friendly living since 1973.
Machynlleth briefly served as the seat of Owain Glyndwr's Welsh Parliament in 1404.
Machynlleth is a key junction on the Cambrian Line, where the Pwllheli and Aberystwyth branches divide.
The Racecourse Ground in Wrexham is recognised as the oldest international football stadium still in use in the world.
Wrexham became Wales' newest city in 2022, granted the status for the late Queen's Platinum Jubilee.
Wrexham General is the main station serving the city.
